Chapter 26

The itinerary: days you can drag

One dndzone per day with svelte-dnd-action, animate:flip for the settling, an optimistic override that is derived rather than synced, place() from the domain on both sides, a stop card, a dialog with assignable deriveds, and a combobox over the gazetteer.

By the end of this chapter

Wire a drag-and-drop library into a live document so the screen shows the drop immediately and agrees with the server when it answers — and build the dialog and search that add stops.

svelte-dnd-action makes a list a drop zone, with the items and a shared type so cards can move between lists. It handles pointer, touch and keyboard — focus a card, press space, arrow — and tells you two things: consider (how the list would look if you dropped here) and finalize (you dropped here). Everything else is ours, and the interesting part is what happens between the drop and the server’s answer.

The library ships an *action*, the shape element behaviour took before attachments arrived in Svelte 5.29: a function applied with use:dndzone={options}, handed the element once and given an update method for new options. This project applies it as an attachment instead, {@attach fromAction(dndzone, () => options)} — fromAction from svelte/attachments turns any action into one — so the zone is attached the same way as everything else in the project, and the difference is worth one sentence: the second argument is a *function* returning the options. The attachment calls it inside an effect of its own, so when group.stops or editable changes, the library’s update runs with the new options, exactly as the action’s would have, and the zone is never torn down. The action used to carry the types of its two events onto the element it was used on; applied through an attachment nothing does, so src/app.d.ts declares onconsider and onfinalize for every element — the augmentation Svelte’s TypeScript guide gives for events that come from an action.

The override. The server is the source of truth and the live query will send the new order a few hundred milliseconds after the drop; in between, the screen should show what the drag said. So override is a copy of the groups with a version stamp, and groups is derived: use the override while the server’s version has not moved past the one we dropped on, and the live groups otherwise. Derived, not synced — there is no effect that copies one into the other and could get out of step. The prop is named view and not state for the reason in the comment: a local called state makes $state read as a store subscription.

Both the zone that lost the card and the zone that gained it fire finalize; only the one that received it — TRIGGERS.DROPPED_INTO_ZONE — sends the move. The move is a day and an index, which is what moveStop takes and what place() in the domain turns into row changes; the server writes them, the live query yields, and the derived groups switches back to the server’s order, which is the same order. If the command fails, the override is dropped and the cards animate back to where the server says they are.

animate:flip on each <li> is what makes the other cards slide out of the way rather than jump; flipDurationMs on the zone tells svelte-dnd-action to expect it, and both read the same duration, which is 0 when the app’s reducedMotion query says so — the one piece of motion in the itinerary that CSS tokens cannot reach. dropTargetStyle: {} turns off the library’s inline outline in favour of dropTargetClasses, a class from the tokens, and transformDraggedElement lifts the library’s clone of the dragged card — a heavier shadow, a degree of tilt. The empty-day item is inside the list so a day with nothing on it is still a drop target, and its sentence tells an editor that it is one. Each day is a rail and a column: the day of the month in the display face, with a hairline running down to the next day. On a phone the heading is the short date — “Sun, May 10” — because the rail beside it already says the day and the weekday, and the long one wrapped onto two lines beside “Add a stop”; both are rendered and a media query shows one, so the server’s HTML is right at every width without a script measuring anything. The title takes the free space (flex: 1 1 0, min-width: 0) and the button none (flex: none), so a long German date wraps instead of squeezing the button’s icon. And above the days sits a visually hidden <h2>: the page’s <h1> is the trip, each day is an <h3>, and an outline that jumps from one to three is a document a screen reader’s heading list cannot make sense of.

A stop that has just arrived lights up once. svelte-dnd-action does not play well with in: transitions on its items, so instead the effect compares the ids with the last render’s and puts a new one in fresh for 1.2 seconds; the card turns data-fresh into a background that fades back over 700ms. fresh is a SvelteSet because it is mutated over time and read by the template; the snapshot it is compared against is a plain Set, because nothing reads it reactively. The first render marks nothing — forty stops do not all light up on load.

The card

The name is a button with aria-pressed, because selecting a stop is a toggle that highlights it on the map — and it is a button’s size: 36px drawn, so the number and the grip centre on it, and 44px to hit, through a pseudo-element that reaches into the card’s padding where there is nothing else to press. The number is the route position from view.scheduled, so the list agrees with the map’s pins. lookers are the companions whose pointer is on this stop, as chips — presence at the granularity of a card. data-kind sets the --kind custom property from tokens.css for the coloured border and the number badge, whose digits are --on-fill — the ink that reads on every kind colour in both themes — so the six kinds of stop share one hue table with the map. On a screen with a mouse the edit and remove buttons fade in on hover or focus; on a touch screen there is no hover, so they are always there. They are hidden by opacity, not display, so a keyboard can still reach them.

The card is a grid with named areas, and the areas change at 40em rather than the markup. On a phone the name has the whole first row and the two actions sit at the end of the second, beside the kind chip; with the buttons on the name’s row, a 360px screen left the name 108px, and the most important words on the screen broke over two lines beside two grey icons. Writing the layout as grid-template-areas makes that decision readable at a glance — the strings *are* the picture — and moving an area is one line in one media query, with no element reordered in the DOM, so the tab order and the reading order stay the same at every width.

The dialog: assignable deriveds

One dialog for adding and editing, told apart by mode, and the fields are assignable $deriveds. Each starts from the stop being edited (or from the day and point the add came from) and is then bound and edited like state; when mode changes — a different stop, or the dialog reopens — every field resets to the new starting value. That is exactly the semantics a form in a dialog wants, and before assignable deriveds it took an effect that copied props into state and a bug when it ran at the wrong time.

The gazetteer is asked for here, by the dialog, when the trip page mounts — long before anybody opens it. places() is the prerender remote function from chapter 17, and the resource it returns has a .current that is undefined until the file arrives and the hundred places after, without suspending anything. The first version awaited it inside the search, and an await in a component with no boundary of its own holds back the update that mounts it: the dialog opened with no search field and the wrong day selected, then rebuilt itself mid-animation when the file landed. Now the first frame of the dialog is its finished layout, and the search shows “Loading places…” in the rare case it is opened faster than a small static file can be fetched. In the browser only: a closed dialog has nothing to render on the server, and the guard keeps the fetch off it.

Why not await with a pending snippet

A <svelte:boundary> with a pending snippet would have kept the rest of the dialog from waiting, and drawn a placeholder where the search goes — a layout that changes when the file arrives, inside a panel that is animating in. Starting the request early and reading .current turns a waterfall (open, then fetch, then render) into a head start, and asks nothing of the layout. await in markup is the right tool when the data *is* the page; here it is a nicety the person may not even use.

Bits UI’s Dialog supplies the focus trap, the Escape key, the scroll lock and the ARIA; the form inside is plain HTML. Saving calls addStop or updateStop — commands, because a dialog only exists once JavaScript is running — and a date change on an existing stop goes through moveStop, the same function a drag uses, so “move to Thursday” means one thing in the whole application. The coordinates are number | null: a stop added with no place picked and no click on the map has no pin, and null says so. The first version started them at 0, 0, which is a real point — in the Gulf of Guinea — and one save of it turned a 1,263km route into a 10,000km one.

Before anything is sent, check() runs the schema the server will run — StopInputSchema or StopPatchSchema, the same import — with v.safeParse, and v.flatten turns its issues into one message per field. A name of three spaces passes the input’s required and fails the schema’s trim; it used to reach the server and come back as a toast of raw JSON, and now it is a line under the field, the field is aria-invalid and aria-describedby points at the line, and nothing is sent. issues is an assignable $derived like the fields, so it resets whenever the dialog opens for something else. The toast for the errors that *do* come back reads errorMessage(error), which the next block is.

A failed command throws SvelteKit’s HttpError in the browser, and an HttpError is not an Error — so the error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error) every component used to write fell through to String(), and the toast read {"status":400,"message":"…"}. isHttpError() from @sveltejs/kit is the test that knows the difference, and body.message is a sentence the server wrote in the request’s language (chapter 21 says how). Anything else — the network went away, a bug — gets the product’s one sentence for “that did not work”, rather than the browser’s English for a failed fetch. Every toast in the trip page goes through this one function, so the rule is in one place. A boundary is the other half of the rule, as the comment’s last paragraph says: its failed snippet is handed an App.Error, which is not an HttpError either, so this function would answer its fallback every time. boundaryMessage, beside it, is the boundary’s half: it reads a message if there is a string one, and falls back to the same sentence if there is not. The end-to-end suite holds the toast to the rule: Ben saves a stop that Ana has just removed, and the toast must say the server’s sentence, “That stop is no longer on the trip.”, whole — not a fragment of it inside a dump of JSON (chapter 43).

Why a guard, and not failed(error: App.Error)

SvelteKit’s documentation writes the snippet as {#snippet failed(error: App.Error)}, and inside SvelteKit an App.Error is what arrives. The annotation does not type-check: Svelte types the snippet as Snippet<[error: unknown, reset: () => void]>, because a boundary is a Svelte feature, and outside SvelteKit — the custom element in chapter 37 — it is handed whatever was thrown. A parameter that claims more than unknown is refused. The way round that the type system offers is a cast, (error as App.Error).message, and a cast is a claim nobody checks: the day handleError returns something else, it compiles and prints undefined. A guard checks — four comparisons, and the snippet relies on exactly what it was handed, a string message or nothing. The trips list, the diagnostics page, the globe and its loader all call it.

The kind is a segmented control — six radios in a fieldset, drawn as a pill track three to a row — six across would squeeze “Transport” and “Hospedagem” out of a 32rem panel — whose chosen segment takes the kind’s colour — and the coordinates sit in a <details> that folds away once a place is picked, because then the pin is already right, and is open while adding: a click on the map gives a pin to nudge, and an add with neither has no pin at all — the summary says “Not set”, the two inputs are required so the browser will not submit, and the summary refuses to fold, because a required field folded out of sight is a form that will not submit and will not say why. The inputs listen for the browser’s own invalid event as well, which unfolds the row and puts the issue under it, and their step is any: a click on the map or a dragged pin gives a coordinate to many more places than four, and step="0.0001" made the browser refuse a perfectly good point as a “step mismatch”. From 40em the dialog opens with focus in the place search, labelled “Place” like every other field (onOpenAutoFocus); on a phone focus stays on the close button, so no keyboard rises over the sheet. The day select writes each day as the itinerary’s headings do — “Sunday, May 10”. The close button is labelled “Close” and the second action “Cancel”: an icon button announced as “Menu”, and a cancel that said “Undo”, were both things a review of the screens caught, and neither shows in a screenshot.

The shell lives in base.css because it is the product’s dialog pattern, not because two dialogs share it today: the stop dialog is the one that wears it. The command palette shares only the scrim — it is a search box you type into, a panel near the top of the screen at every width, not a sheet — and its own comment says so. On a phone the shell is a bottom sheet with a grabber, sliding up on the --ease-sheet curve; from 40em it is a centred panel that rises 8px and scales from 96%. There is no JavaScript in any of it: Bits UI sets data-state="open" while the dialog is up and closed as it leaves, waiting for the exit animation, so the motion is two keyframe rules per state — and under reduced motion every --dur-* is zero and the dialog simply appears.

A combobox over the gazetteer

Bits UI’s Combobox is the accessible half — role="combobox", a listbox, arrow keys, Escape, type-ahead, aria-activedescendant. The other half is ours: the places arrive as a prop, already loaded or still empty, and matches filters a hundred names on every keystroke without a server. The component used to fetch them itself, with $derived(await places()); the dialog above says why that moved out. query is read from the input’s own event because the root’s inputValue is a prop to set, not one to bind — the kind of detail a headless library’s docs say once.

Checkpoint

  • You can explain the override, why it is derived, and what the version stamp compares against.
  • You can say which finalize sends the move and why the other one must not.
  • You can describe assignable deriveds in the dialog and what they replaced.
  • You can say why the gazetteer is fetched by the dialog and read through .current, rather than awaited by the search.
